question: What is an ANR? How do you avoid them?
answer:
An ANR fires when the main thread fails to respond in time — roughly five seconds for an input event.

The system raises one when:
• An input event has not been handled within about 5 seconds.
• A BroadcastReceiver has not returned within ~10s in the foreground or ~60s in the background.
• A service started with `startForegroundService` does not call `startForeground` within its timeout.
• `Service.onCreate` / `onStartCommand` or a ContentProvider call overruns.

Avoid them by never blocking the main thread:
• Move I/O, database work and heavy CPU off main with coroutines and `Dispatchers.IO` / `Default`.
• No `Thread.sleep`, no `runBlocking`, no `.get()` on a future on the main thread.
• Watch for the blocking calls that do not look blocking: synchronous IPC (`Binder.transact`), the first SharedPreferences read, a Room query accidentally left non-suspend, inflating a huge layout, decoding a bitmap during scroll.
• Turn on `StrictMode` in debug builds so disk and network on main fail loudly while you develop.
• Profile with a system trace (Perfetto, from the Android Studio profiler) and look at the worst frames, not the average.

Diagnose in production with Play Console Vitals, which gives the main-thread stack at the moment of the timeout, and read `ApplicationExitInfo` on the next launch to find out why the previous process died — it reports ANRs, crashes and low-memory kills with the trace attached.

question: How do you find and fix memory leaks on Android?
answer:
A leak on Android is almost always something long-lived holding on to a destroyed Activity, Fragment or View.

Where they come from:
• A static field or singleton holding a `Context` — pass `applicationContext` to anything that outlives a screen.
• Inner classes and lambdas capturing `this` — a delayed `Handler` callback, a listener, a Runnable.
• Listeners registered with a system service, an event bus or a third-party SDK and never unregistered.
• Fragments keeping a `View`, a view binding or an adapter past `onDestroyView` — the fragment outlives its view tree, so the binding must be nulled there.
• Coroutines in `GlobalScope`, or a `CoroutineScope` you created yourself and never cancelled.
• Large bitmaps and drawables cached in a static field.

Find them:
• LeakCanary in debug builds — it watches destroyed Activities, Fragments, ViewModels and Services, and when one stays reachable it prints the exact reference chain holding it.
• Android Studio's Memory Profiler — rotate a screen a few times, capture a heap dump, and look for more than one instance of the same Activity.
• `adb shell dumpsys meminfo <package>` for a quick size check, and Play Vitals for real-user OOM rates.

Fix by shortening lifetimes rather than sprinkling `WeakReference`: scope work to `viewModelScope` / `lifecycleScope`, unregister in the matching lifecycle callback, use `DisposableEffect` in Compose, and keep state in a ViewModel that is cleared for you.

question: What is jank? How do you measure and fix dropped frames?
answer:
Jank is a frame that misses its deadline, so the display shows the previous one again and the user sees a stutter.

The budget is one refresh interval — about 16.7ms at 60Hz, 8.3ms at 120Hz — shared between your main-thread work and the RenderThread.

Measure:
• While developing — a system trace (Perfetto) from the Android Studio profiler. Every frame is a slice on the frame timeline, janky ones are flagged, and you can see which call overran.
• In CI — Macrobenchmark with `FrameTimingMetric`, which reports P50/P90/P99 frame durations for a scripted journey, so a regression fails the build instead of shipping.
• In production — the `JankStats` library reports per-frame durations from real devices, tagged with the state you attach (which screen was on top).
• Quick check — `adb shell dumpsys gfxinfo <package> framestats`.

Common causes and fixes:
• Work on the main thread during scroll: image decoding, JSON parsing, disk reads. Move it off and prefetch before the row is visible.
• Compose — reading state too high in the tree so a whole screen recomposes; unstable parameters that defeat skipping; allocating in a composable. Defer reads into lambdas (`Modifier.offset { }`, `graphicsLayer`), hoist state no higher than it needs to go, give `LazyColumn` items a stable `key`, and check the recomposition counts in Layout Inspector.
• Views — deep hierarchies and overdraw. Flatten with ConstraintLayout, drop redundant backgrounds, and use `DiffUtil` with stable ids so RecyclerView rebinds only what changed.
• The first frames of a screen running interpreted instead of compiled — that is what a baseline profile fixes.

question: What does R8 do to a release build, and what breaks when its keep rules are wrong?
answer:
R8 shrinks, optimizes and obfuscates your code in a single pass over the bytecode when you build a release variant. It replaced ProGuard as the default years ago, so `minifyEnabled` today means R8.

What it does:
• Shrinking — walks the reference graph from the entry points named in the manifest and drops every class, method and field nothing reaches.
• Optimization — inlining, dead-code elimination, class merging, devirtualization, constant folding, all whole-program.
• Obfuscation — renames what survives to short names, which shrinks the DEX further and makes casual reverse-engineering harder.
• Resource shrinking (`shrinkResources`) — removes drawables and strings no surviving code references.

Full mode is the default in current AGP: R8 optimizes more aggressively and assumes less about reflection than the old ProGuard-compatibility mode, so a library that used to work may now need explicit keep rules.

What breaks is anything resolved by name at runtime — reflection, JNI lookups, `Class.forName`, Gson's field names, class names sent to analytics. Those survive only if a rule keeps them. Most libraries ship consumer rules and need nothing from you, so when a release build crashes and the debug build does not, a missing `-keep` is the first suspect. Keep rules are also the reason a release APK can be larger than it should be: `-keep class com.app.** { *; }` disables shrinking for your whole app.

Always test the release variant before shipping, and upload `mapping.txt` to Play or Crashlytics — without it every production stack trace reads `a.b.c`.

question: What are baseline profiles and what do they buy you?
answer:
A baseline profile lists the methods ART should compile ahead of time at install, instead of interpreting them on first run.

Without one, a fresh install runs your code interpreted and JIT-compiles it as it goes, so the first launch and the first scroll are the slowest the app will ever be. Google measures roughly 30% faster cold start and visibly smoother first scrolls on real apps.

How you get one:
• Add the `androidx.baselineprofile` Gradle plugin and a benchmark module.
• Write a `BaselineProfileRule` test that drives the critical journeys — launch, scroll the main list, open a detail screen.
• Run `./gradlew :app:generateBaselineProfile` on a rooted emulator or an unlocked device; the plugin writes the rules into the app module and AGP packages them into the APK or AAB.
• Verify with Macrobenchmark: measure `StartupTimingMetric` with `CompilationMode.None()` against `CompilationMode.Partial()` and compare, rather than trusting that it helped.

`includeInStartupProfile = true` additionally produces a startup profile, which lets AGP reorder the DEX so startup classes sit together and fewer pages are faulted in.

Two things to say if asked what it does not do: it changes nothing on a device that has already run the app for a while (ART's own profile takes over), and Play separately distributes a cloud profile aggregated from real users, which combines with yours. Regenerate it when the critical journeys change — a stale profile just precompiles code nobody runs.

question: How do you optimize app startup time on Android?
answer:
Cold start is the case that matters: the process, the Application object and the first Activity all have to be created before anything reaches the screen.

• Cold — no process exists. Everything is built from scratch.
• Warm — the process is alive, the Activity has to be recreated.
• Hot — the Activity is still in memory and is only brought forward.

Measure:
• Logcat prints `Displayed com.app/.MainActivity: +XXXms` for the first frame.
• `adb shell am start -W` reports `TotalTime` for one launch.
• Macrobenchmark with `StartupTimingMetric` gives time-to-initial-display and time-to-full-display across iterations, on a device you choose.
• Play Vitals and Firebase Performance give the real-user distribution, which is where slow devices show up.

Where the time actually goes:
• `Application.onCreate` initializing SDKs. Defer everything not needed for the first frame — the App Startup library, a lazy initializer, or work posted after the first frame.
• ContentProviders: every library that declares one is created before `Application.onCreate`, and you pay for it whether or not you use the library. App Startup exists to collapse them into a single provider.
• Your code running interpreted on first launch — ship a baseline profile.
• Blocking the first frame on data. Use `installSplashScreen()` with `setKeepOnScreenCondition` only while it is genuinely necessary, and call `reportFullyDrawn()` (or `ReportDrawn` in Compose) when real content is up, so the platform and Play measure time-to-full-display correctly instead of stopping at an empty skeleton.
• Layout work done twice — a deep view hierarchy, or a Compose screen that recomposes on every intermediate state during load.

A reasonable target: `Application.onCreate` well under 200ms, and the first meaningful frame under a second on a mid-range device.
